demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette:
Gerald Kowalski is a 62-year-old married man of Polish-American descent who has worked as a bank teller at a regional branch in suburban Ohio for nearly two decades. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after the incident that brought him here, describing himself as a man who had "never needed this kind of help before" and who remains visibly uncomfortable with the idea that he does now.

The event occurred on a Tuesday afternoon last autumn. Gerald was driving home from a weekend errand, moving through a residential intersection he had navigated hundreds of times, when his attention shifted for a moment toward his phone mounted on the dashboard. In that interval, his vehicle struck a cyclist - a man Gerald recognized immediately when he got out of the car: his neighbor's adult son, someone he had watched grow up, someone whose name he had known for twenty years. The young man sustained a severe traumatic brain injury and spent weeks in intensive care. He survived, but his recovery has been long and incomplete, and Gerald was present at the scene for nearly forty minutes before the ambulance arrived, kneeling beside him, speaking to him, watching.

In the weeks that followed, Gerald continued to go to work, continued to sit across the teller counter from customers, continued to come home to his wife, Diane. But something had reorganized itself beneath the surface of that routine. He began sleeping in fragments, lying rigid in the dark with a quality of alertness he could not switch off, as though some part of him remained stationed at that intersection. Even in his own living room, in a chair he had sat in for thirty years, he could not settle into the kind of ease that used to come naturally. He described it as feeling like a man waiting for something, though he could not say what.

The memory itself did not behave like other memories. It arrived in pieces - the sound of the impact, the particular color of the cyclist's jacket, the texture of the asphalt under his knees - surfacing without invitation and vanishing before he could orient himself to them. When he did recall the event more fully, the terror he had felt on that pavement returned with it, not as a distant echo but as something immediate and physiological. Alongside the terror came guilt of a quality he found almost unbearable, a guilt that did not diminish with time or reassurance.

At work, the difficulties became concrete and cumulative. Gerald's position requires sustained interaction with people he knows - this is a small community branch, and many of his customers are regulars, some of them neighbors, some of them friends of the family whose son he struck. When a familiar face appeared at his window, something in Gerald tightened acutely. He began requesting shifts that were less likely to bring in the neighborhood clientele, and his supervisor had noticed and asked questions he deflected. When a colleague placed a hand briefly on his shoulder during a difficult transaction, he flinched so sharply that the woman apologized and kept her distance afterward, and Gerald was mortified in a way that lingered for days.

He had come to believe, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that he was not the same man he had been before the accident - that whatever the event had done to him was not temporary but structural, a permanent alteration in his capacity to function. He was certain that his inability to sleep properly, to relax, to stop scanning the environment for threats he could not name, reflected something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. A competent man, he reasoned, would have recovered by now. The fact that he had not was evidence, to him, of an inadequacy he had perhaps always carried but never been forced to confront.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a conversation with Diane, who told him quietly one evening that she missed him - not that he was absent, but that he was unreachable, even when sitting beside her. He was most afraid, he said in his intake session, that she was right, and that nothing could change it.
